description: We are a multidisciplinary team bridging the gap between orbital technology and biological innovation. By leveraging NASA’s open-source satellite data and cutting-edge space science, we aim to monitor, analyze, and protect living ecosystems from above. Our mission is to transform complex planetary data into actionable insights for a sustainable future, proving that the answers to Earth's biological challenges often come from the stars.
summary: Bio Orbit is a concept for a compact, modular space farming system designed to grow fresh food inside spacecraft and orbital habitats. The project explores how plants can be cultivated without traditional soil using hydroponics, nutrient-rich water, LED grow lights and environmental monitoring sensors. The system uses a controlled growing chamber, water reservoir, pump, airflow system and sensors to support plant growth while maintaining containment. It aims to supplement packaged food, reduce dependence on fresh food resupply and support crew wellbeing during long-duration space missions. The project also demonstrates how water-efficient and controlled-environment farming concepts used in space can contribute to sustainable agriculture on Earth. Bio Orbit is an educational prototype concept and not a certified spaceflight system.
details:
Bio Orbit is a compact, modular hydroponic farming concept designed to support fresh food production in spacecraft and orbital habitats.

The system works through a controlled growing chamber where plants are supported using net pots, seedling holders and inert growing media instead of ordinary soil. A water reservoir stores nutrient-rich water, which is circulated to the plant roots through a small pump and tubing system. A return mechanism is designed to collect and reuse the water.

LED grow lights provide the light required for photosynthesis, while a small fan supports air circulation. Temperature, humidity and water-level sensors help monitor growing conditions. A microcontroller such as Arduino can read sensor information and control the lights, fan and pump.

The suggested starter crops include lettuce, spinach, basil and microgreens because of their compact size and relatively short growing cycles.

The project aims to demonstrate how controlled-environment agriculture can supplement packaged food, reduce dependence on fresh food resupply and support crew wellbeing during long-duration missions.

Bio Orbit also has applications on Earth, including indoor farming, urban agriculture and water-efficient food production.

The project combines hydroponics, environmental monitoring, sustainable resource management and basic automation. Important challenges considered include microgravity water management, power consumption, heat control, hygiene, plant health and system reliability.

This is an educational concept and prototype design. Its proposed water-return mechanism and other systems would require further testing before any real spaceflight application.
